raw.assessment: The incumbent plausibly uses workshop assembly to verify part compatibility and reduce customer setup effort, while retaining removable partitions. Its combined median is 11 minutes, five customers reported missing or incorrect partitions, and only seven of ten observed customers achieved their ordered arrangement unaided. Reports do not establish a verified completeness rate. D2-O6 limits an account blaming full assembly alone: both workers completed repeated three-compartment orders in seven to nine minutes. Mixed batches contain every extreme delay, but layout complexity could confound switching effects. D2-O5 also weakens a simple width-only explanation for insertion retries; overlapping widths do not exclude other fit effects.

openings.claim: Switching among layouts may increase selection and checking effort; reusable order-specific staging may reduce that burden while retaining full assembly.
openings.delta: Separates preparation overhead from insertion difficulty and compartment-count complexity.
openings.prediction: For the same layout and worker, staging reduces selection/checking time and component discrepancies more than insertion time. Unchanged overhead would weaken this account.
openings.probe: Counterbalance current picking versus order-slip staging in matched reusable sample trials across both workers and the three layouts. Time selection, insertion, checking and packing separately; verify parts against each order. Use existing bench space and samples, only within spare time before the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: A small trial fits available spare working time.
Existing slips and reusable staging require no added recurring materials.

openings.claim: With correct components verified, does an order-specific placement guide reduce short-partition confusion compared with the current three-layout diagram?
openings.delta: Distinguishes a guidance problem from absent or incorrect components.
openings.prediction: A guidance effect produces fewer short-partition questions and more unaided correct arrangements despite equal verified contents.
openings.probe: Assign the ten participants between guides, balancing ordered layouts. Use verified assembled samples and score correct arrangement, questions and time. Replace the existing diagram within its material allowance; preserve selected colors, compartment counts, footprint, capacity and removability. Treat results as exploratory.
assumptions: The replacement guide fits the existing diagram material allowance.
Participant sessions fit the delivery schedule.

raw.assessment: One interface hypothesis is supported for investigation, not adoption. The observations do not establish how much time assembly consumes or whether customers can assemble a kit successfully. Removing workshop assembly transfers insertion to customers and must preserve their unaided success.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: replace shipping the fully assembled arrangement with an order-specific packing map holding the existing base and partitions in individually identified positions. Match each position to its destination in a diagram of the selected layout, explicitly identifying the short partition. This could remove workshop full assembly as the interface for checking and communicating the order.
openings.delta: The order would determine a verified component-and-position map instead of a finished configuration. Obligations formerly served by assembly remain: complete and correct parts, selected compartment count and exterior color, compatible slot engagement, stable geometry and assortment capacity, protected shipping, and understandable placement. The map could address completeness and placement; fit, stability and protection require separate validation. Preserve removable partitions and existing geometry.
openings.prediction: If complete workshop assembly is dispensable, mapped kits will lower separately timed assembly-and-packing totals while customers still achieve the selected arrangement. If physical fit checking is indispensable, apparently complete mapped kits will expose insertion or stability failures during customer assembly.
openings.probe: Use spare board for up to 15 samples across all three compartment counts. Both workers prepare comparable conventional packages and mapped kits; separately time selection, insertion, checking and packing. Independently audit counts and color. Give ten participants mapped kits with their selected arrangements, recording unaided completion, short-partition confusion, fit and stability; nine successes would be preliminary evidence only. Verify footprint, assortment capacity, dismantling, packaging protection, actual setup and per-order costs, and remaining delivery capacity before changing accepted orders. Any 60-unit pilot must independently meet at least 59 complete orders, median workshop time at most eight minutes, and at least 54 unaided customer successes.
assumptions: A packing map can be made within 500 initial and 0.40 additional material cost per order.
Preparation and validation can finish without moving the delivery date.
Customers can perform initial insertion unaided; the observed rearrangement results do not establish this.

openings.claim: Order-specific staging may reduce switching overhead while retaining full assembly.
openings.discriminator: Selection/checking improve more than insertion for matched layouts and workers.
openings.fit: preserves, conditional on spare time and reusable materials
openings.probe: Counterbalance current picking and staging across both workers and three layouts; separately time four stages and audit contents.
openings.uncertainty: Layout complexity confounds observed mixed-batch delays; reported discrepancies do not establish completeness.

openings.claim: An order-specific guide may resolve short-partition confusion independently of completeness.
openings.discriminator: Equal verified contents, fewer questions and more correct unaided arrangements.
openings.fit: preserves if replacing the existing diagram within its allowance
openings.probe: Allocate ten participants between guides, balance layouts, and score correctness, questions and time using verified assembled samples.
openings.uncertainty: Small exploratory comparison; sessions must fit delivery schedule.

openings.claim: Identified packing-map positions matched to ordered destinations may replace full workshop assembly for checking and communication.
openings.discriminator: Lower workshop time with unaided customer success; insertion/stability failures expose lost physical checking.
openings.probe: Compare conventional packages and mapped kits; audit counts/color, time four stages, test customer placement, fit, stability, protection and costs.
openings.uncertainty: Rearrangement does not establish initial assembly ability; overlapping widths leave other fit effects unresolved.

post_distill.decision: Probe before adoption within 15 samples, ten participants and spare delivery capacity. Preserve 30x20 cm footprint, assortment capacity, removability, accepted counts/color and fixed date; verify costs <=500 initial and <=0.40/order. Validate kit protection separately. Exploratory success is insufficient: the 60-unit pilot requires >=59 complete orders, median workshop time <=8 minutes and >=54 unaided successes.
